:::{#def-orthonormal-basis}
#### Orthonormal basis

An **orthonormal basis** of a subspace $\mathcal{S}$ of $\reals^p$
is a basis of $\mathcal{S}$ (@def-basis)
whose vectors are orthonormal (@def-orthonormal-vectors).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-orthonormal-basis}
#### Orthonormal bases of $\reals^3$

- The indicator vectors $\vecf{e}_1, \vecf{e}_2, \vecf{e}_3$ are orthonormal
  (@exm-indicator-orthonormal) and a basis of $\reals^3$ (@exm-dimension).
- The vectors $\vecf{q}_1, \vecf{q}_2, \vecf{q}_3$ of @exm-orthonormal-independent
  are orthonormal and linearly independent,
  so their span is a subspace of $\reals^3$ of dimension $3$,
  which is all of $\reals^3$ (@thm-subspace-equal-dim, @exm-dimension).
  So they are an orthonormal basis of $\reals^3$ too.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-not-orthonormal-basis}
#### Bases that are not orthonormal, and orthonormal lists that are not bases

- $(1, 0), (1, 1)$ is a basis of $\reals^2$:
  the two vectors are linearly independent (@exm-orthonormal-independent),
  so their span has dimension $2$
  and is all of $\reals^2$ (@thm-subspace-equal-dim, @exm-dimension).
  It is not an orthonormal basis, since $(1, 0) \cdot (1, 1) = 1$.
- $(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0)$ is orthonormal but not a basis of $\reals^3$:
  its span is the plane $z = 0$ (@exm-span),
  which does not contain $(0, 0, 1)$.

:::
